title1: CT Foundation Models as Feature Extractors for Lung Cancer Prediction: A Multicohort Study
title1b: Encoder, Classifier and Selection Choices for Frozen CT Foundation Models in Lung Cancer Tasks: A Multicohort Analysis
summary1: Across multiple CT cohorts and lung cancer prediction tasks, frozen foundation models generally outperformed a random-weight encoder but rarely surpassed nodule diameter, the Brock model or radiomics, highlighting the importance of strong clinical comparators and external validation.
key_points1: In this retrospective study of 18 foundation models across 12 public CT cohorts (12993 nodules or tumors; 7265 participants), the selected foundation model setup had areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.82 (95% confidence interval: 0.80, 0.85) in the LUNA25 challenge development set and 0.72 (95% confidence interval: 0.69, 0.76) in the Duke Lung Cancer Screening Dataset, compared with 0.82 (95% confidence interval: 0.80, 0.85) and 0.73 (95% confidence interval: 0.69, 0.77) for nodule diameter.

In exploratory external screening and radiologist suspicion analyses, 90.0% (95% confidence interval: 78.6%, 94.4%) of foundation model setups had higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve point estimates than a random-weight encoder, whereas 4.3% or fewer exceeded nodule diameter, the Brock model or radiomics.

Adding the selected foundation model score to nodule diameter changed the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve by −0.003 (95% confidence interval: −0.033, 0.027) in the Duke Lung Cancer Screening Dataset and +0.017 (95% confidence interval: −0.002, 0.035) in the LUNA25 challenge development set; none of the three prespecified primary hypotheses was supported after Holm adjustment.
summary1b: Across lung cancer prediction tasks, the choice of frozen CT foundation model encoder mattered more than the classifier, and model setups chosen with test labels or tested only within the training cohort gave optimistic performance estimates.
key_points1b: In this retrospective study of 18 frozen CT foundation model encoders in 16 lung cancer prediction tasks (7265 participants), the encoder and its interaction with the task explained 22.1% and 23.7% of the variance in external test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and the classifier 0.6% (post hoc).

No alternative classifier exceeded logistic regression in external testing, and one encoder chosen by rank in other tasks did not differ from a full search (difference in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, +0.002 [95% confidence interval: −0.025, 0.027]; post hoc).
For the same model setups, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was lower in external testing than within cohorts (−0.031 [95% confidence interval: −0.044, −0.022]; post hoc).
